title: Perform primary meat inspection incisions of pork

lessons.title: Planning and preparing for pork inspection
lessons.html:
Purpose

Primary inspection incisions of pork are prescribed by the regulations under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. They expose lesions of pork measles (Cysticercus cellulosae), tuberculosis-like lymphadenitis, abscesses and other conditions that cannot be seen from the surface. Because the human tapeworm Taenia solium can cause serious disease in people, including cysticercosis of the brain, careful pork inspection is an important public health measure in South Africa, especially for pigs from free-range or backyard systems.

Preparing the station

  • Bright lighting at the head, pluck, viscera and carcass inspection points.
  • Head presentation: in pork the head is often left attached to the carcass or kept matched to it. Make sure the head and the masseter muscles are accessible.
  • Pluck and viscera presentation that keeps organs matched to the carcass number.
  • Sterilizer at the correct temperature, hand-wash basin, two knives, a steel and a hook.
  • Detention rail, tags and condemned containers.
  • PPE: clean clothing, apron, boots, head cover, cut-resistant glove where required.

Planning

  1. Check the ante-mortem record: fevered, lame or tail-bitten pigs, and pigs from sources with a measles history.
  2. Agree with the line supervisor on stopping the line and diverting carcasses.
  3. Check that line speed allows the full routine.

Pork-specific considerations

  • Pork is usually dressed with the skin on, so skin lesions such as erysipelas diamonds, bite wounds and scalding faults are visible.
  • The lungs of pigs can contain scald water if the pig was not dead and fully bled when scalded.

lessons.title: Performing the incisions on pork
lessons.html:
Routine sequence

Follow the fixed sequence and number of incisions in which you were trained. The main parts are:

Head and throat

  • Observe the head, skin, snout and mouth.
  • Incise the mandibular (submaxillary) lymph nodes. Look for enlargement, abscesses and caseous or calcified lesions. In pigs these nodes are an important site for detecting tuberculosis-like lymphadenitis.
  • Incise the masseter muscles with long, flat cuts to search for measles cysts.
  • Observe and palpate the tongue; measles cysts may be visible or felt under its surface.

Pluck

  • Observe and palpate the lungs; incise the bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes. Look for pneumonia, pleurisy, abscesses and scald water.
  • Open the heart sac and examine the heart; incise the heart as prescribed to look for measles cysts and endocarditis.
  • Observe and palpate the liver for milk spots, abscesses and cysts; incise the portal lymph nodes as prescribed.

Viscera

  • Observe the stomach, intestines and spleen. Observe and palpate the mesenteric lymph nodes; incise if abnormal.

Carcass

  • Observe skin, cut surfaces, pleura, peritoneum and diaphragm. The diaphragm pillars and exposed muscles are checked for measles cysts.
  • Observe the kidneys for haemorrhages, which can indicate septicaemia or swine fever.
  • Check joints, the spine and the tail area for abscesses spreading from tail bites.

Technique

  • Clean, decisive cuts; no hacking.
  • Sterilise after every carcass and immediately after cutting a lesion.
  • Keep all parts matched.

lessons.title: Completing the pork inspection
lessons.html:
Putting the findings together

Look at the findings from all parts together. A measles cyst found in one masseter means the whole carcass must be detained and examined further according to the regulations. Haemorrhages in skin, kidneys and lymph nodes together suggest generalised disease or a controlled swine fever.

Actions

FindingAction
No abnormalityContinue to marking
Milk spots in liver onlyRemove or trim liver as regulations allow; carcass continues
Localised pleurisyMark pleura and lungs for removal
Measles cyst foundDetain carcass with all parts; refer
Lesions in submaxillary nodesDetain; examine other nodes; refer
Scald water in lungsCondemn lungs; report to supervisor (welfare and bleeding issue)
Suspected swine feverStop, detain, report immediately

Controlled diseases

If a controlled disease is suspected, follow the abattoir's emergency procedure and the instructions of the veterinarian. The Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 requires reporting. Do not allow any part of the suspect carcass or related carcasses to leave.

Records and follow-up

  • Record carcass number, producer, findings and actions.
  • Record measles cases carefully; traceback to the farm is important for human health.
  • Report dressing faults, such as scald water in lungs, which signal welfare problems at sticking and bleeding.

Key points

  • Pork measles is caused by the larva of Taenia solium and is a serious human health risk.
  • Incise the masseters, examine the tongue, heart and diaphragm for measles.
  • Incise the mandibular (submaxillary) lymph nodes for lymphadenitis.
  • Check kidneys and skin for haemorrhages that may indicate swine fever.
  • Detain all parts of suspect carcasses and record every finding.
